theme: God’s patience with rebellion; David chosen as shepherd-king
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 78:40-72. This is the second half of the history psalm. It continues from the wilderness through the plagues of Egypt, the conquest, the failures in the land, and ends with the choice of David. Notice how the story ends.
settingTheScene: Psalm 78 continues. Verses 40 to 72 go back over the exodus, with the plagues, and then move forward through the settlement in the land, Israel’s idolatry, the capture of the ark, God’s rejection of Shiloh, and his choice of Judah and David. It is a summary of the story from Exodus to 2 Samuel, and it ends with a hopeful note.
observation: “How often they rebelled against him in the wilderness and grieved him in the desert!” (v. 40).
“They did not remember his power or the day when he redeemed them from the foe” (vv. 42-43).
The plagues of Egypt are named: blood, flies, frogs, locusts, hail, pestilence, and the death of the firstborn (vv. 44-51).
“Then he led out his people like sheep and guided them in the wilderness like a flock” (v. 52).
“Yet they tested and rebelled against the Most High God and did not keep his testimonies” (v. 56).
“They provoked him to anger with their high places; they moved him to jealousy with their idols” (v. 58).
“He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where he dwelt among mankind, and delivered his power to captivity” (vv. 60-61).
“He chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds… to shepherd Jacob his people… With upright heart he shepherded them and guided them with his skillful hand” (vv. 70-72).
interpretation:
The second half of the psalm shows what happens in the land. The pattern from the wilderness continues. God brings them in, but they test him again and turn to idols. Judgment follows: the ark is captured and Shiloh falls. These are events from the period of Samuel that you will read about soon. The psalm sees all of it as a single pattern: grace, rebellion, judgment, and then, remarkably, grace again.

The surprise comes at the end. After a long account of failure, the psalm does not end with destruction. It ends with the choice of David. “He chose David his servant.” The LORD wakes up like a man who has been asleep and chooses a new shepherd for his people. The humble beginnings are important. David is taken “from the sheepfolds, from following the nursing ewes.” God’s way is to raise up the unlikely.

The picture of the king is a shepherd. “He shepherded them with upright heart and guided them with his skillful hand.” This is the model for leadership in Israel: a shepherd who cares for the flock. It is the same image that opens the wilderness section: “He led out his people like sheep.” The one who led Israel through the desert through Moses will now lead them through David.

For anyone who has read the whole story from Genesis to Deuteronomy, the psalm gives a long view. The failure is real, and God’s judgment is real, but his plan is not defeated. He is working toward the shepherd king, a descendant of David, who will lead his people perfectly.

The lesson for the next generation is that God’s faithfulness is the thread in the story. Our failures are not the point. His mercy is. That is what the children are to be taught.
connection: Jesus is the Son of David and the good shepherd (John 10:11). Matthew 9:36 says that when he saw the crowds, “he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.” Ezekiel 34:23 promises that God will set one shepherd over them, his servant David. In 1 Peter 5:4, Jesus is called the “chief Shepherd.” Hebrews 13:20 calls him “the great shepherd of the sheep.”
application:
Reflect on the pattern in your own story: grace, failure, discipline, and grace again. Thank God for his steadiness.

Think about who has shepherded you spiritually. Thank them, and pray for them.

Ask how you might shepherd those entrusted to you, with a pure heart and skillful hands.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus, the good shepherd who laid down his life.
Ask God to help you tell the story of his faithfulness to those near you.
Thank him for choosing and leading shepherds for his people.
